title: Shared services VPC bridge and conditional egress playbook
content:
Purpose:
This doc captures design options, tradeoffs, and a lightweight runbook for implementing a shared‑services VPC bridge pattern with conditional egress for customer POC/private deployments. Intended audience: solutions engineering, infra, customer SREs, and security reviewers.

Scope and constraints:
- Cloud-focused (AWS primary), notes for GCP/Azure callouts in later sections.
- Targets customer POCs and early production houses where customers want private networking + selective external egress.
- Emphasizes minimal changes to customer network while keeping Redwood Private deployment safe and observable.
- Not covering full IAM/compliance checklist (see linked Confluence).

Assumptions:
- Customer runs workloads in their VPC(s) and wants Redwood inference nodes reachable via private connectivity (PrivateLink or VPC peering/transit).
- Customer may require all model calls to egress through a monitored, customer-controlled proxy (e.g., for DLP, traffic inspection) or allow selective direct egress for telemetry endpoints.
- We control a ‘shared-services’ VPC that hosts model-serving endpoints in Private deployment mode.
- Team has permission to create VPC endpoints, route tables, security groups, and resolver endpoints in customer account when doing on-prem/VPC integrations (with least privilege).

Goals:
- Provide a repeatable pattern for connecting customer VPCs to Redwood Private with clear options for ingress and egress control.
- Allow conditional egress routing (per-customer or per-route) with observable health/fallbacks.
- Minimize cross-account network blast radius.

Pattern variants (quick overview):
1) PrivateLink (VPC Endpoint Service) + Customer Endpoint (recommended for strict isolation)
   - Pros: Enforced AWS PrivateLink semantics, no route table or IGW exposure, per-service endpoints, good for multi-account isolation.
   - Cons: Requires endpoint creation on customer side; TLS termination decisions needed; limited cross-AZ cost; cannot proxy non-TCP easily.

2) Transit VPC / Transit Gateway with route-based segmentation (good for fleets and many customers)
   - Pros: Centralized routing, easier to manage many VPCs, supports more complex routing policies.
   - Cons: Higher blast radius, more complex NACL/SG modelling, may require peering/transit setup by customer infra.

3) Simple VPC Peering (fast POC option)
   - Pros: Quick to stand up for single-customer PoC, predictable L3 connectivity.
   - Cons: No transitive routing, more manual route updates, visibility limitations.

4) Hybrid: Peering to a customer-managed ‘onramp’ VPC that contains NAT/proxies and resolver endpoints; Redwood peers to that onramp.
   - Pros: Minimal touch inside customer app VPC; customer can manage egress policy centrally.
   - Cons: Additional VPC to operate, slightly more latency.

DNS model options (Route53-centric examples):
- Private hosted zone per customer with conditional forwarding to Redwood Route53 inbound resolver in shared-services VPC. Use Route53 resolver rules to forward *.redwood-private.example -> inbound-resolver-ip.
- Split-horizon: customer DNS resolves internal names to private IPs; Redwood uses Route53 resolver outbound rules to resolve customer internal hosts.
- Endpoint service discovery: Use endpoint-specific CNAMEs published to customer; or provide static IPs + health check records.

Conditional egress strategies (customer requirements drive choice):
A) Full egress via customer proxy (strict security):
   - Pattern: Customer requests all outbound from the inference nodes to go through their proxy. Setup: peer/shared VPC route table points 0.0.0.0/0 -> customer NAT/proxy IP (onramp). Attach network ACLs + SG to force traffic.
   - Fallback: If proxy unreachable, use a secondary path to Redwood-managed egress with customer approval (manual/automated failover).

B) Split egress (recommended for lower ops):
   - Pattern: Only a whitelist of external destinations (e.g., telemetry, metrics endpoints) allowed via customer egress; other destinations blocked or sent via Redwood managed egress. Implement using route table prefixes and policy-based routing on the onramp.

C) No external egress (air-gapped/regulated):
   - Pattern: All outbound blocked; Redwood nodes allowed only to communicate with customer internal services and Redwood control plane via approved peering. Use NACLs + SGs to enforce.

Endpoint types and TLS termination choices:
- PrivateLink with TLS passthrough: Redwood requires the client to perform mTLS to the service. Good for zero-trust.
- PrivateLink with TLS termination at the service: Redwood terminates TLS; customer sees PrivateLink connection only. Simpler for some customers but requires trust.
- TLS via SNI proxy for multi-tenant hostnames on single endpoint IP (careful with certificate management).

Security controls and observability:
- Security groups should be principle of least privilege: only allow customer CIDR(s) to ports used by inference (e.g., 443/8443).
- NACLs as defense-in-depth for egress restrictions on subnets hosting Redwood nodes.
- VPC Flow Logs to central logging (customer’s or Redwood’s logging endpoint) with 7‑day hot retention and 90‑day cold storage recommendations for POC.
- Endpoint health checks: active probes from both sides; publish probe endpoints in a shared health page (internal).
- Audit: log endpoint creations (PrivateLink), route table changes, and resolver rule changes to a joint access log (S3) with lifecycle policy.

Workshop notes (customer workshop run during POC kickoff):
- Attendees: customer infra lead, customer security engineer, Redwood SEs (Arjun, Maya), SRE (Priya).
- Agenda: map existing customer VPCs, identify internal DNS patterns, list external egress requirements, pick pattern variant, sketch rollback plan.
- Outcome: customer preferred Hybrid onramp with split egress; required that all telemetry to third parties go via their proxy; agreed to create route and resolver permissions for us to test.

Step-by-step POC runbook (minimal, for SE-run POC):
1) Prep (day -3 to -1): share architecture diagram and minimal IAM template. Create ticket PROJ-4821 for coordination.
2) Customer creates a connectivity sandbox VPC (CIDR suggestion 10.101.0.0/16) and an onramp bastion/proxy instance/NLB.
3) Create PrivateLink service in Redwood shared-services VPC, enable acceptance mode or whitelist customer account ID.
4) Customer creates VPC endpoint and associates subnets; validate route tables and SGs.
5) DNS: create resolver rule in customer account to forward redwood-private.* -> inbound resolver IP. Test dig/nslookup from customer app host to redwood service name.
6) Egress: configure route in onramp to send traffic for approved external prefixes to the customer proxy. Configure explicit deny for other 0.0.0.0/0 if required.
7) Observability: enable VPC Flow Logs and a temporary packet capture (tcpdump) on the onramp instance for troubleshooting (time-bounded).
8) Smoke tests: run simple inference call patterns (sync/streaming) and observe latency and error modes.
9) Failover test: intentionally block proxy and verify routing/fallback behavior; document errors and expected client semantics.
10) Post-mortem and Handover: update Confluence, create runbook entries for onboarding additional customers.

Testing checklist for SEs:
- DNS resolution both directions (customer->redwood, redwood->customer internal services).
- TLS handshake verification and SNI behavior across PrivateLink.
- Throughput test 100 RPS sustained for 5 minutes with KV cache verify.
- Egress policy enforcement: probe allowed and disallowed destinations.
- Flow logs and health events emitted and visible in expected S3/CloudWatch endpoints.

Rollback and incident playbook (short):
- If connectivity causes production impact: withdraw route change on customer onramp -> cut traffic to a safe hold (customer-designated sandbox route).
- If PrivateLink acceptance misconfigures: remove endpoint service or revoke permissions and notify customer.
- For DNS blowups: revert resolver rules and test with host-level overrides (hosts file).

Open questions & action items:
- Q: Does customer require per-tenant egress accounting at token-level? (Action: Arjun to follow up, due 2025-09-05).
- Q: Should Redwood offer a managed onramp AMI for customers? (Action: Product evaluation, Priya to prototype).
- Action: Add explicit test for mTLS between customer and Redwood endpoints (Sofia, 2025-09-01).
- Action: Draft minimal IAM CloudFormation template for endpoint creation and resolver permissions (Maya, 2025-08-20).

Appendix — quick reference commands:
- Test DNS from EC2: dig +short redwood-private.service.customer.internal @<resolver-ip>
- Validate PrivateLink: aws ec2 describe-vpc-endpoints --filters Name=service-name,Values=com.amazonaws.vpce.<redwood-service>
- Temporarily capture traffic on onramp: sudo tcpdump -i eth0 -w /tmp/onramp.pcap port 443 or host <customer-proxy-ip>

References and related pages:
- Confluence: Shared Services VPC Patterns (linked_artifacts)
- Jira: PROJ-4821 (POC coordination)
- GitHub: infra template PR #2416 (linked_artifacts)

Notes to self / informal fragments from the workshop:
- Customer wants a single outbound audit log for regulatory team — suggest splitting telemetry to a separate subaccount or S3 bucket with KMS.
- Watch out for cross-account resolver quotas (Route53 inbound/outbound per account quotas).
- Consider offering an optional hardened onramp AMI with iptables-based egress controls for customers who can’t run a proxy.
